about: The rubrics call the sentence before Pater noster the preface of the Lord's Prayer. After et ne nos indúcas in tentatiónem, they assign the response sed líbera nos a malo to the server. At low Mass the faithful may say the whole Our Father with the priest, in Latin, and add the Amen with him.

seg.tr: Taught by precepts that lead to salvation and formed through divine instruction, we dare to say:

ex.w009: “Audémus dícere” expresses filial boldness: instructed by Christ, we dare to say “Our Father.”

seg.nr: The priest spreads his hands, and keeps them so through the prayer.

seg.tr: Our Father, who art in heaven,

ex.w016: Latin speaks here of “the heavens” in the plural. The received English keeps the familiar “in heaven”.

seg.tr: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us this day our daily bread.

ex.w032: Latin says literally “give us our bread”. The English prayer preserves the same direct object.

seg.tr: And forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.

ex.w041: Latin “débita” means literally “debts”. The received English speaks of “trespasses”.
ex.w047: Literally: debtors, those who owe us something. The received English speaks of those who trespass against us.

seg.tr: And lead us not into temptation,

ex.w059: This edition parses “malo” as the neuter noun for evil. The following embolism takes it up in the neuter plural, “ab ómnibus malis.” The Catechism also explains that the petition ultimately refers to the Evil One (CCC 2851).

nt.w059: The form is the ablative of both words at once. It can be malum, evil as a thing, or malus, the Evil One. Neither the form nor the sentence decides, and the tradition reads it both ways. This edition takes malum and marks the doubt.
